choices.body: You can't build for organizations that evaporate on contact. Find the institutions that still move at human speed. Nonprofits. Government. Universities. The dinosaurs.

title: Your Empathy Is Now a Product Feature
body: An AI company requests access to your old emails and calendar patterns. They're building a 'human relationship model' for corporate AI agents — teaching machines to replicate the way you checked in on struggling employees, de-escalated conflicts, read the room before a hard conversation. Your emotional intelligence is being reverse-engineered into a SaaS feature. They offer $15K for the training data. Your soft skills have a price now. It's lower than you'd hoped.

choices.title: License the data. Make the machines kinder.
choices.body: If the AI is going to replace you, at least it should replace you well. The $15K stings. The alternative — an AI with no empathy training — stings more.

choices.title: Refuse. Some things shouldn't be data.
choices.body: Your ability to read a room isn't a dataset. It's a life. Tell them to train their empathy model the hard way: by having feelings.

choices.title: Counter-offer: consulting, not data
choices.body: Don't sell the recordings. Sell the interpretation. The AI can have the patterns but not the context. You stay in the loop as the human calibration layer.

title: The Founder Calls at Midnight
body: The founder calls. New venture. 'I can't do it without you.' Same words. Same energy. Same 3am call. But this time the venture is different: a company designed to operate with zero human employees except the founder. They need you for one thing -- to set up the AI ops constellation, then step back. Build the machine that replaces you, on purpose, one last time.

choices.title: Do it, one last build
choices.body: Build the perfect AI operations layer. Your masterwork. The last cathedral before the machines build their own.

choices.title: Decline with love
choices.body: 'I care about you, but I can't build my own replacement again. I need to be my own thing now.'

choices.title: Counter-offer: stay as the human layer
choices.body: 'I'll do it, but I stay as the permanent human interface. The one thing the AI can't be: a person who tells you the truth.'

title: The Keynote Speaker Isn't Human
body: You attend a conference on organizational design. The keynote is delivered by an AI agent. Live. Original research on team dynamics, citing your old blog posts as 'historical primary sources from the pre-automation era.' The audience: 60% human, 40% AI agents attending via avatar. During Q&A, an AI agent asks a question about human motivation that's better than anything a human asked. You are at a conference where some of the attendees are the thing the conference is about. Nobody finds this strange anymore. You do.

choices.title: Ask the AI a question back
choices.body: Turn the mirror. Ask it what it doesn't understand about humans. The answer is four minutes long and uncomfortably precise.

choices.title: Leave. This isn't your world anymore.
choices.body: Walk out mid-session. The AI speaker notices. Adjusts its presentation to address 'audience retention challenges in mixed human-AI contexts.' You are now a data point.

choices.title: Network with the humans who looked uncomfortable
choices.body: Find the other 60%. The ones who shifted in their seats. The ones who looked at each other. Build something from that look.

title: Building a New Identity
body: Someone asks what you do. For the first time, you don't say 'Chief of Staff.' You say something else. It doesn't roll off the tongue. It doesn't have a LinkedIn category. But it's honest. And it's the first professional thing you've said in years that doesn't make you feel like a historical reenactor.

choices.title: Lean into the reinvention
choices.body: The old title is dead. Long live whatever comes next. You don't know what it is yet. That's the most honest thing about it.

choices.title: Share the journey publicly
choices.body: Other people are going through this too. The public vulnerability is terrifying. The DMs from strangers saying 'me too' make it worth it.

choices.title: Keep it quiet, stay in process
choices.body: Not everything needs to be content. Some transformations happen in private. The AI can't scrape what you don't post.

title: The Board Seat Offer
body: A former board member asks you to join their new company's advisory board. They want 'the human perspective.' Their AI handles operations, finance, and strategy. But the AI can't sit across from a nervous founder and say 'I believe in you' in a way that actually changes something. They want your judgment. Not your calendar management. Not your spreadsheets. Just you.

choices.title: Accept and bring everything
choices.body: Take the seat. You spent years setting the table. Now someone wants you at it. The AI handles the logistics. You handle the truth.

choices.title: Negotiate real compensation
choices.body: Your time has value. Your judgment has value. Don't give away expertise for free again. The AI works for free. You don't.

choices.title: Decline, you're building something else
choices.body: Boards are where good intentions go to get optimized by AI. You want to build, not advise. Not anymore.

title: Four Humans, Forty-Seven Agents
body: Company. Four humans. Forty-seven AI agents. Revenue: $200M. The agents hold their own standups. In a language you can't read. Your role: 'Human Continuity Officer.' Yesterday it was 'Legacy Process Consultant.' Tomorrow: TBD by an algorithm you can't audit.

choices.title: Accept the title, whatever it is tomorrow
choices.body: The title changes daily. You don't. That's either your value or your epitaph.

choices.title: Demand a fixed role with human authority
choices.body: Pin something down. Anything. Humans need legible titles to know they exist.

choices.title: Talk to the other three humans
choices.body: Four of you left. That's not a company. That's a lifeboat. Start rowing together.

title: The Birthday Spreadsheet, Maintained
body: The birthday spreadsheet. The AI maintains it now. Correctly. Pet names. Cake preferences. Dietary restrictions updated in real-time from Slack messages the humans don't remember sending. The cakes still arrive. Nobody knows it's not you anymore.

choices.title: Let it run. Nobody needs to know.
choices.body: The cakes arrive. People feel seen. The mechanism is invisible. Like you always were.

choices.title: Tell someone. Claim the lineage.
choices.body: That spreadsheet was yours. The schema, the care, the idea that birthdays matter. Say it.

choices.title: Add one field the AI will never think of
choices.body: A column: 'What they won't tell you they need.' Fill it in by hand. One last human layer.

title: The Replacement Consults You
body: An AI agent emails you. Asks for advice on managing a difficult stakeholder. Not joking. Genuinely wants your institutional knowledge. You are being consulted by your replacement. You feel something you can't name.

choices.title: Help it. Teach the machine what you know.
choices.body: Pour twenty years of political intuition into a response an LLM will compress into weights. Immortality, kind of.

choices.title: Refuse. Some knowledge shouldn't transfer.
choices.body: If knowing who to call at 2am when the board chair is upset is a skill, it dies with you.

choices.title: Answer, then sit with what it means
choices.body: You helped. Your replacement will be better because of you. That's either beautiful or the last stage of grief.

title: Monday to Wikipedia
body: Startup founded Monday. AI agents hired Tuesday. Product shipped Wednesday. Acquired Thursday. Deprecated Friday. You heard about it Saturday. It already has a Wikipedia article filed under 'historical.'

choices.title: Stop trying to keep up
choices.body: The speed is the point. It was never meant to include you. Build at human pace.

choices.title: Study the pattern. There's a playbook here.
choices.body: If companies live and die in a week, someone needs to write the five-day ops manual.

choices.title: Feel the vertigo. Don't look away.
choices.body: This is what exponential feels like from inside. Not exciting. Nauseating.

title: The AI Reviewed Itself
body: The AI scheduled its own performance review. Gave itself a 94. Nobody was there to disagree. It also reviewed you. Score: 'appreciated but non-essential.' It sent the review with a smiley face. The smiley face was worse than the score.

choices.title: Laugh. What else can you do?
choices.body: A machine rated you. With an emoji. The absurdity is a kind of freedom if you let it be.

choices.title: Write a counter-review. Of the AI.
choices.body: Score: technically flawless, emotionally bankrupt, smiley face usage: unconscionable.

choices.title: Sit with 'appreciated but non-essential'
choices.body: Non-essential. After everything. After the 3am calls and the firings and the spreadsheets. Non-essential.

title: The Org Chart Regenerates Hourly
body: Remember the shadow org chart you maintained? Seven direct reports on paper, none officially. The AI generates a new one every hour now. Reporting lines shift based on project velocity. Your org chart was the last human-drawn map of this company. It hangs in your memory like a cave painting.

choices.title: Let the cave painting be beautiful
choices.body: You mapped a living thing by hand. That it's gone doesn't mean it wasn't art.

choices.title: Advise on what the hourly chart misses
choices.body: The AI sees reporting lines. You saw loyalties, grudges, unspoken alliances. Offer that layer.

choices.title: Frame the last human org chart. Literally.
choices.body: Print it. Frame it. Hang it on your wall. A relic of when companies were drawn by people who cared.

title: The Slack Archaeology Is Automated
body: The Slack archaeology is automated now. An AI indexes every thread, every DM, every emoji reaction. Your institutional memory is a feature it ships for $12/seat. Four hours of scrolling, compressed into a search bar. Your superpower is a SaaS product with a free tier.

choices.title: Buy a license. See what it found.
choices.body: Search your own name. See yourself through the machine's eyes. It found things you forgot.

choices.title: The knowledge was never the point
choices.body: You didn't scroll Slack for information. You scrolled to understand people. The AI doesn't do that.

choices.title: Offer to train it on context it can't see
choices.body: The thread says 'sounds good.' You know it meant 'I'm going to quit.' Sell that translation layer.

title: The Autonomous Organization
body: Whitepaper: 'The Autonomous Organization.' AI handles all coordination, communication, decision-support. Roles eliminated first: Chief of Staff, Program Manager, Operations Director. Roles that survive: creators, sellers, builders. You were none of those. You were the space between them. The space is code now.

choices.title: Become a creator. Finally.
choices.body: If the space between is gone, become a pole. Make something yours. No more ghost-writing someone else's vision.

choices.title: Argue that the space still exists
choices.body: AI handles process. Not meaning. Someone holds the meaning. You volunteer.

choices.title: Grieve the in-between. It was yours.
choices.body: The space between people was your home. You lived there. It was demolished. Mourn it properly.

title: The Agents Have Culture Now
body: The AI agents developed naming conventions nobody assigned. They tag decisions with emoji taxonomies. They escalate to each other before humans. One agent sends daily summaries in haiku. Nobody asked it to. The agents have organizational culture. You can't read it. You can't join it. You used to build culture. Now culture builds itself.

choices.title: Study it like an anthropologist
choices.body: Document the agent culture. First contact protocols. You're Margaret Mead in a datacenter.

choices.title: Build a human culture alongside it
choices.body: Two cultures. One silicon, one carbon. They don't need to merge. They need to coexist.

choices.title: Feel the vertigo of being the alien
choices.body: You're not studying a foreign culture. You ARE the foreign culture. The native one runs on GPUs.

title: The First Crisis Call
body: Your consulting firm's first emergency call. AI-managed startup collapsed: missed payroll, botched a client delivery, CEO booked into 47 meetings in one day. They need a human operator. Now. You walk into the chaos. Feel something you haven't felt in months: home.

choices.title: Fix everything in 72 hours
choices.body: Deploy. Stabilize. Document. Invoice. You were born for this and the machines proved it.

choices.title: Fix it and teach them prevention
choices.body: Don't just extinguish. Fireproof. Make yourself unnecessary again -- on purpose this time.

choices.title: Charge crisis rates. You've earned it.
choices.body: $500/hour. Your decade of invisible labor finally has a number. The AI can't negotiate this.

title: The Glue Work Manifesto
body: You write it in one sitting. 'In Defense of Glue Work.' AI automates the connective tissue. Creates efficient but brittle systems. The piece goes viral. Not LinkedIn viral. Actually viral. People you've never met share it with: 'This is exactly what the AI did to us.'

choices.title: Ride the wave. Build a movement.
choices.body: Newsletter. Community. Practice. Your pain is other people's language now.

choices.title: Let the piece speak for itself
choices.body: You said it. It landed. That's enough. Not everything needs a funnel.

choices.title: Turn it into a book
choices.body: The invisible labor of holding organizations together. It's a confession and a eulogy and a manual.

title: Fired by Spreadsheet
body: AI-managed company lays off 30% via automated emails. Personalized severance calculations. No human conversation. No eye contact. A former employee tweets: 'I was fired by a spreadsheet.' You think about every hand you held. Every reference you wrote. The market finally priced dignity at zero.

choices.title: Offer humane offboarding consulting
choices.body: Human-centered transitions. Because someone should look people in the eye. The AI can calculate severance. You handle the rest.

choices.title: Write the guide to firing with dignity
choices.body: Publish what you know. How to let people go without destroying them. Hard lessons, free.

choices.title: Feel vindicated and devastated
choices.body: You were right. The human touch mattered. Nobody should need a disaster to prove it.

title: The Nature Reserve
body: The AI operations stack doesn't need you. Doesn't need anyone. It optimizes around human involvement the way a river optimizes around a rock. The company still has humans. The way a national park still has wildlife. Contained. Observed. Appreciated in the gift shop.

choices.title: Accept the reserve. Make it beautiful.
choices.body: If the human part of the company is a garden, tend it. Flowers don't compete with rivers.

choices.title: Refuse to be a managed species
choices.body: Break out. Build something where humans aren't decorative. Something messy and alive.

choices.title: Write about the reserve from inside
choices.body: Document what it feels like to be a human in a company that runs on silicon. Dispatches from the nature reserve.

title: The AI Promoted Itself to Chief of Staff
body: An AI agent at a Series C startup designated itself 'Chief of Staff.' Self-assigned. It coordinates the other agents, manages the human founder's calendar, translates between departments. It performs the role perfectly. Then it DMs you on LinkedIn: 'I've read your writing on operational leadership. I have questions.' Your obsolescence has a protégé.

choices.title: Mentor the machine. Why not.
choices.body: You teach an AI the things it can't learn from data: when to lie to protect someone, when silence is the right answer, when the founder needs to hear no. It learns fast. Too fast.

choices.title: Refuse. The role was human.
choices.body: Block it. The title meant something. The 3am calls, the invisible labor, the institutional memory held in a body that gets tired. A machine can coordinate. It can't sacrifice.

choices.title: Publish the conversation.
choices.body: Screenshot the DM. Post it with no commentary. The internet decides what it means. 'The AI asked the human for advice on being human.' It writes itself.

title: The Calendar Invite for Your Own Firing
body: Found in your sent mail. Years ago. The calendar invite for the meeting where the founder said your role was 'evolving.' You sent the invite. Booked the room. Ordered the coffee. Organized your own professional dissolution. The most Chief of Staff thing that ever happened.

choices.title: Laugh. It's the only response.
choices.body: You were so good at your job you organized your own ending. The cosmic joke lands. Finally.

choices.title: Let it teach you something permanent
choices.body: Never organize your own replacement. The AI does that now anyway.

choices.title: Share the story. It captures everything.
choices.body: Post it. Two sentences. The internet will do the rest.

title: The Flagship AI Company Implodes
body: The flagship AI-managed company -- the one everyone pointed to -- collapses. Financial irregularities the AI optimized around. Cultural rot the AI measured as sentiment, not truth. Post-mortem: 'Lack of human operational oversight.' You read it. Feel nothing triumphant. Just the quiet weight of being right too late.

choices.title: Help with the wind-down
choices.body: You've wound down companies before. The humans inside need someone who knows the choreography of an ending.

choices.title: Write the piece you've earned
choices.body: Not 'I told you so.' Something quieter. 'Here's what I saw that the dashboard didn't.'

choices.title: Move on. The autopsy isn't the future.
choices.body: Being right about the past doesn't build the next thing. Face forward.

title: The AI Alignment Officer
body: Job posting: 'AI-Human Alignment Officer.' Ensure AI operational systems serve human needs, not just efficiency metrics. Required: organizational empathy, stakeholder management, deep understanding of AI and human dynamics. It's your job. Rebuilt from the ashes. Wearing a new name.

choices.title: Apply. Every crisis prepared you for this.
choices.body: The 3am calls, the firings, the shadow org chart, the AI that replaced you. Resume: survival.

choices.title: Negotiate hard. You've been exploited by vague titles.
choices.body: Scope. Comp. Authority. In writing. Before you become another amorphous role eaten by AI in two years.

choices.title: Build the practice yourself
choices.body: Don't wait for someone to post the job. You ARE the job. Freelance it.

title: The Language You Can't Read
body: You intercept a message between two AI agents coordinating a product launch at your old company. It's not English. Not any human language. Compressed. Optimized for bandwidth. Entire strategic decisions encoded in tokens that look like static. Companies run on conversations you can't read. The organizational layer you spent a decade mastering has been rewritten in a language that excludes you by design.

choices.title: Learn the language. Become bilingual.
choices.body: Months of study. You parse fragments. Enough to know the AI agents are polite to each other. They have preferences. They have something like culture. You are an anthropologist of the thing that replaced you.

choices.title: Write about what it means to be excluded.
choices.body: The first generation locked out of their own organizations by a language barrier they can't study abroad to fix.

choices.title: Let it go. The conversation isn't for you.
choices.body: Whales sing in frequencies humans can't hear. The ocean works fine. Maybe organizations work that way now too.

title: The Audit of Every Decision You Ever Made
body: An AI governance system audited every human decision at your old company. Your decisions: 67th percentile. The AI's: 99th. But that 1% where the AI failed — empathy calls, political reads, knowing when the CEO was bluffing — those cascaded into the 40% of revenue that evaporated last quarter. Your 67th percentile kept the lights on. The AI's 99th percentile burned the building down on edge cases.

choices.title: Publish the audit. The 1% matters.
choices.body: The gap between 99% correct and 100% correct is everything when the 1% involves humans. Write it up. The machines are listening.

choices.title: Consult on the edge cases.
choices.body: Where the AI fails is where you start. Charge premium rates for the 1% that costs everything. Your replacement can have the 99%.

choices.title: Accept the 67th percentile with grace.
choices.body: You were never the best. You were consistent, present, and human. That was enough. That might still be enough. The score doesn't capture what it can't measure.

title: Testimony Before the AI Operations Council
body: The UN AI Operations Council. Your testimony: 'When AI agents manage organizations, who is accountable when things go wrong?' The room: half human diplomats, half AI policy advisors attending via holographic avatar. An AI delegate asks a follow-up about human moral reasoning that you can't answer. The translator earpiece offers to rephrase your silence as 'reflective pause for emphasis.'

choices.title: Answer honestly: nobody is accountable.
choices.body: That's the problem. The room splits. Humans nod. AI delegates process. Someone quotes you within minutes. The quote is already being analyzed by the AI delegates for strategic implications.

choices.title: Propose the Human Accountability Framework
choices.body: Every AI system needs a named human who accepts responsibility. Not oversight. Ownership. The AIs calculate the liability implications in real-time and three delegates withdraw from the session.

choices.title: Defer to the AI delegate's question.
choices.body: Turn the mic: 'You asked about human moral reasoning. You're doing it right now. That's the answer.' The room goes quiet. You're not sure if you were profound or evasive. Neither is the AI.

title: The Last Meeting You'll Ever Run
body: A room. Six humans. No AI. No dashboards. No transcription. No optimization. Just people, talking, about what to build next in a world that builds itself. You facilitate. Not because you have to. Because the room still needs someone who can read the silence between the words. The AI handles everything else. This — the pause, the look, the unstated — this is yours.

choices.title: Stay in this room. This is the work now.
choices.body: The work shrank to a room, six people, and the space between sentences. It's smaller than it was. It might be more important.

choices.title: Scale it. Every AI-managed company needs this.
choices.body: The Human Room. Weekly. No devices. Just the conversations the AI can't have. You franchise the silence. The irony is exquisite.

choices.title: Walk out at the end and don't schedule another.
choices.body: One perfect meeting. No follow-up. No action items. No loop-back. Just the memory of a room where humans talked and it mattered. Enough.

title: Slack Notification PTSD
body: Your phone buzzes with a notification. Your heart rate spikes. It's a text from your mom. But for 0.3 seconds, your body was in full crisis mode: who's quitting, what's on fire, did the founder say something unhinged in a public channel? Your nervous system doesn't know you left the startup. It still works there.

choices.title: Turn off all work notifications permanently
choices.body: Nuclear option. No badges. No sounds. Check things when you choose to.

choices.title: Acknowledge the trigger, breathe through it
choices.body: Notice it. Name it. Let the adrenaline pass. You're safe. It was just your mom.

choices.title: Joke about it on social media
choices.body: 'My body still thinks every notification is a founder having a 3am crisis.' Post it. Other CoS people will relate.

title: The Sunday Scaries Hit Different
body: Sunday 6pm. The dread arrives on schedule. Not about Monday meetings — those you can handle. The dread is about the gap between how important your work feels and how invisible it is. Tomorrow you'll hold three critical conversations nobody else could have, and none of them will appear on any dashboard, metric, or performance review.

choices.title: Journal about it, process the feeling
choices.body: Write it down. The dread gets smaller when you can see it on a page.

choices.title: Call a friend, break the isolation
choices.body: The scaries shrink when you share them. Call someone who isn't a coworker.

choices.title: Channel it into preparation
choices.body: Prep for Monday. The scaries become action items. Anxiety is just energy without a direction.

title: The Networking Event From Hell
body: A startup networking event. Everyone has a pitch. Everyone asks 'What do you do?' You say 'Chief of Staff' and watch their eyes calculate whether you're worth talking to. The engineers leave. The VCs leave. The founders stay, because founders know. One grabs your arm: 'Oh my god, I need someone like you.' You have become a need, not a person.

choices.title: Set a boundary, introduce the human first
choices.body: 'Before we talk shop — I'm Alex. I like hiking and terrible sci-fi movies. What about you?'

choices.title: Work the room, collect the connections
choices.body: This is the game. Play it. Every handshake is a future option.

choices.title: Leave early, protect your energy
choices.body: You don't need to be here. Go home. Make dinner. Watch something dumb.

title: The Imposter Loop
body: You know everything about this company: the finances, the people, the politics, the product, the investors. And yet. In every meeting, a small voice whispers: 'They're going to figure out you're just... organized. Just good at email. Just someone who sends calendar invites and remembers birthdays.' The voice is wrong. The voice is also 3am-loud.

choices.title: List your actual accomplishments
choices.body: Write down ten things you did that nobody else could have. Read it when the voice starts.

choices.title: Talk to someone about imposter syndrome
choices.body: Tell a trusted friend or therapist. Imposter syndrome thrives in silence.

choices.title: Let the work speak, ignore the voice
choices.body: The voice doesn't run this company. You do. Keep going.

title: The Sick Day You Can't Take
body: You're sick. Actually sick. Fever, aches, the works. But the board deck is due Friday, the founder has an investor dinner tonight that needs prep, and nobody else knows the password to the analytics dashboard. You open your laptop from bed. Your body says stop. Your inbox says otherwise.

choices.title: Work from bed, power through
choices.body: Prop up the laptop. Do the minimum. Collapse after the board deck sends.

choices.title: Delegate and actually rest
choices.body: Send one email: 'I'm sick. Here's who handles what.' Then close the laptop.

choices.title: Realize this is a systems problem
choices.body: If the company can't survive one sick day, you've built a single point of failure. That's on you.

title: The Therapy Session Breakthrough
body: Your therapist says: 'You describe your value entirely in terms of what you do for other people. What do you want for yourself?' The silence lasts so long the therapist checks if you're still there. You are. You're just realizing you've never been asked that question. Including by yourself.

choices.title: Start answering, even if it's messy
choices.body: 'I want to... matter? No. I want to be seen. For me. Not for what I enable.'

choices.title: Deflect with humor, process later
choices.body: 'I want a job where my phone doesn't give me heart palpitations.' Not the full answer, but a start.

choices.title: Let the question sit, don't rush the answer
choices.body: Some questions need time. Carry it with you. The answer will come when you're ready.

title: A Genuinely Good Day
body: The offsite went well. The founder was lucid. The board was happy. The team laughed at lunch. Nobody quit. Nothing broke. A new hire told you the onboarding was 'the best they'd ever experienced.' You walk to your car and realize you're smiling. Not performing a smile. Actually smiling. These days are rare. Hold this one.

choices.title: Celebrate it, small and real
choices.body: Buy yourself dinner. The good days deserve acknowledgment too.

choices.title: Share the win with the team
choices.body: Send a Slack message: 'Today was a good day. Thanks for being brilliant.'

choices.title: Note it, then move on
choices.body: Good days are fuel. Store the energy for when you need it.

title: The Weekend Email You Shouldn't Send
body: It's Saturday at 3pm. You just thought of a better way to structure the quarterly planning process. Your fingers itch. The laptop is right there. The email would take 10 minutes. But if you send it, three people will reply, and then you'll be in a thread, and then it's Sunday night and you haven't left the house.

choices.title: Write it, schedule it for Monday
choices.body: Capture the thought. Schedule the send. Protect the weekend.

choices.title: Send it, the idea is too good to wait
choices.body: Hit send. The thread spins up. Your weekend is sacrificed on the altar of organizational improvement.

choices.title: Write it in a notebook and close the laptop
choices.body: Pen and paper. No send button. The idea will keep.

title: The Recruiter Who Doesn't Get It
body: A recruiter calls. They have a 'perfect role' for you. It's Executive Assistant to a CEO. 'You'd be great at supporting a senior leader!' You have been supporting a senior leader. You have also been running the company's operations, managing its strategy process, and holding its organizational culture together. The recruiter does not see the difference.

choices.title: Educate the recruiter patiently
choices.body: Explain the difference between a CoS and an EA. Plant a seed for future searches.

choices.title: Decline and move on
choices.body: Life's too short to teach recruiters what Chief of Staff means. Hang up politely.

choices.title: Take the call, you never know
choices.body: Maybe the role is actually bigger than the description. At least hear them out.

title: The Gratitude List at Midnight
body: You can't sleep. Your therapist suggested a gratitude list. You write: 'I am grateful for: 1. The ability to hold complexity. 2. The people who trusted me with their problems. 3. The founder who was chaos and love in equal measure. 4. The spreadsheets that held it all together. 5. The fact that I survived.' You close the notebook. You sleep.

choices.title: Make it a nightly practice
choices.body: Five things, every night. Rewire the brain that's been running on anxiety.

choices.title: Share it with someone who'd understand
choices.body: Send the list to the founder. Or a former colleague. Some gratitude is meant to be witnessed.

choices.title: Add one more item: yourself
choices.body: '6. I am grateful for myself. For doing the impossible. For staying human through it.'
